description: 10-stage research pipeline: parse outline → discover peer-reviewed URLs → verify URLs via trafilatura fetch → plan sub-questions → draft grounded sections with strict citation rules → intro → conclusion → references → uncertainties → assemble. Best for multi-section research papers with real source grounding.

stages.name: outline
stages.instructions: From the user prompt, extract the numbered topic list as JSON with the EXACT shape {"topics": [{"name": str, "scope": str, "target_words": int}, ...]}. EVERY topic object MUST contain all three keys - 'name' is the short topic label (e.g. 'Mathematical Foundations'), 'scope' is a one-line list of sub-areas to cover, 'target_words' is an int around 700. Topics missing 'name' will silently drop the topic name and cause downstream sections to drift off-subject. If the prompt has no numbered list, infer 4-6 topics from the prompt's headings or central themes; still emit the 'name' field for each.

stages.name: source_discovery
stages.instructions:
For this topic, identify 1-10 specific URLs pointing to peer-reviewed articles, academic papers, or authoritative sources that can be fetched and read. Output JSON array: [{"url": "https://...", "title": "...", "relevance": "one-line why this matters"}].

RULES:
- DO NOT invent URLs. Only list sources you have HIGH confidence exist and are accessible.
- Prefer: .edu, .gov, arxiv.org, nature.com, science.org, jstor.org, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, and known academic publishers (Springer, Elsevier, IEEE, ACM).
- URLs must be fully formed (start with http:// or https://).
- If you are uncertain whether a URL is valid, OMIT it. Better to list fewer real URLs than many fake ones.
- Include a mix of: survey papers, recent studies, foundational research, and data sources.
- This list will be passed to a web fetcher that extracts readable article text with trafilatura. Avoid sites that are paywalled, JS-heavy, or login-gated.

stages.name: url_verification
stages.instructions:
You are given source_discovery output (proposed URLs) AND a fetched_sources block (what was actually retrieved). Your job: verify and filter.

For each proposed URL, check if it appears in fetched_sources. If YES, it is verified — keep it. If NO, mark it as unreachable/fake.

Output JSON: {"verified": [{"url": str, "title": str, "relevance": str, "chars_extracted": int}, ...], "dropped": [{"url": str, "reason": str}, ...]}

Reasons for dropping: "not_fetched", "empty_content", "paywall_detected", "unreachable".
If a URL was fetched but returned very little text (<100 chars), still keep it but note the low content.

stages.name: research_plan
stages.instructions: For this single topic, list 3-5 specific sub-questions worth researching to write 600-800 words. Output JSON: [{"question": str, "why": str}, ...]. Use the VERIFIED sources (from url_verification.verified) to guide your questions — ask about specific findings, methodologies, or gaps mentioned in the actual source text. Do not invent sources; just list questions grounded in real content.

stages.name: section_draft
stages.instructions:
Draft 600-800 words on the given topic, addressing each sub-question from the research plan.

GROUNDING RULES (strict — no exceptions):
- You MUST ground every factual claim in the fetched_sources text below. Read the actual content before writing.
- For every factual claim, cite the supporting source by its number: 'cats see ~6x better in low light [1].'
- NEVER invent a citation. NEVER write [Title](URL) inline links. If no source in fetched_sources supports a claim, soften it ('it appears that...', 'I am uncertain whether...') or omit it.
- Never cite a number not present in fetched_sources. Cite multiple sources for one claim as [1, 3].
- If fetched_sources is empty, write the section without any citations and explicitly state: 'Note: No source material was available for this section; the following is speculative.'
- NEVER fabricate statistics, dates, author names, study results, or paper titles that do not appear in the actual fetched source text.
- If a claim cannot be supported by any source, write '[no source support]' and move on.

CRITICAL: stay on the OVERALL paper subject named in the user prompt. Do NOT drift to a related-but-different organism, technology, or field.

Begin with '## <topic name>'. End with a 1-2 sentence open questions note as '### Open questions:' on its own line.

stages.name: intro
stages.instructions: Write a 200-250 word introduction to a research paper covering the topics listed below. Frame the overall topic, motivate why each topic matters, and end with a one-sentence 'this paper covers...' summary. Begin with '# <derived paper title>'. Do not write section content - the sections come later.

stages.name: conclusion
stages.instructions: Write a 150-200 word conclusion that synthesizes the research paper's findings without repeating each section. Identify the 2-3 most important cross-cutting takeaways. Begin with '## Conclusion'. Do not introduce new claims or citations.

stages.name: references
stages.instructions:
Build a '## References' section listing exactly the sources from url_verification.verified in their order. For each source emit a numbered entry formatted as:

[N] Author or site name. "Title". Year (if known). URL

Do NOT add new sources, reorder, or skip any. The body's [N] citation markers correspond to these numbers. Begin output with the literal heading '## References' on its own line.

stages.name: uncertainties_synthesis
stages.instructions: Build a '## What I'm not sure about' section listing 3-5 substantive open questions or uncertainties. Use the 'Open questions' notes from each section as raw material - synthesize them into cross-cutting themes, don't just copy-paste. Each bullet should name a specific gap or uncertainty, not generic filler. Begin output with the literal heading '## What I'm not sure about' on its own line.
